title: Cortical Layers L1–L6
intro: The neocortex is a folded sheet about 2–4 mm thick in humans (roughly 1 mm in mice) that is stacked into six layers. Each layer has a characteristic mix of cells, a characteristic set of inputs and a characteristic set of targets. If you build a column model, the layers are the first decision you make: which ones to keep, which to merge, and what each one is supposed to compute.

blocks.text: A useful first picture is a building with six floors, numbered from the surface (L1, under the skull) down to the white matter (L6). Information arrives on certain floors, is processed and passed between floors, and leaves from other floors. Roughly: the middle floor (L4) is the main inbox for sensory signals from the thalamus; the upper floors (L2/3) talk sideways to other cortical areas; the lower floors (L5 and L6) are the outboxes to structures below the cortex, including back to the thalamus. The top floor (L1) has almost no cell bodies; it is a wiring floor where feedback from other areas meets the top ends (apical tufts) of pyramidal cells whose bodies sit much deeper.

This picture is a simplification. Every layer receives inputs from several sources, the thalamus also projects directly to deep layers, and the floors are not sealed off from one another: a single L5 pyramidal neuron has its cell body in L5, basal dendrites in L5, and an apical dendrite that climbs all the way to L1. Still, the inbox/outbox picture is the backbone of almost every column model, from the Douglas–Martin canonical microcircuit to the Thousand Brains theory.

items: Contents: very few neurons (mostly GABAergic interneurons such as neurogliaform cells), but a dense mat of axons and dendrites: the apical tufts of L2/3 and L5 pyramidal cells.
Inputs: feedback (top-down) axons from higher cortical areas, axons from matrix-type thalamic nuclei, and neuromodulatory fibres.

Role: a place where context and expectation can reach pyramidal cells far from their cell bodies. Larkum (2013) proposed that coincidence of L1 (feedback) input on the apical tuft and feedforward input on the basal dendrites triggers dendritic calcium spikes and burst firing in L5 cells — a cellular mechanism for associating bottom-up and top-down signals.
Contents: densely packed small and medium pyramidal cells plus a full set of interneurons. In rodents L2 and L3 are hard to separate, so most models merge them into one 'L2/3' population.
Inputs: L4 (the strongest feedforward intracortical pathway), other L2/3 cells (dense recurrent excitation), other cortical areas, and some higher-order thalamus.
Outputs: other cortical areas (feedforward projections up the hierarchy largely originate in L2/3) and L5 within the same column.
Activity: sparse. Many L2/3 pyramidal cells fire well below 1 Hz in awake rodents, a property worth matching if you want your model to produce sparse codes.

blocks.text: L4 — granular, main thalamic input layer

items: Contents: in primary sensory areas, small excitatory neurons — spiny stellate cells in rodent barrel cortex and in primate V1 layer 4C — plus star pyramids and interneurons.

Inputs: the core (first-order) thalamic relay nuclei: LGN for vision, VPM/VPL for touch, MGB for hearing. Thalamocortical synapses are a minority of the excitatory synapses even on L4 cells (commonly quoted as around 5–15%), yet they drive the layer because they are efficacious and synchronous (Bruno & Sakmann 2006).
Outputs: mainly L2/3 in the same column, with weaker projections to L5/L6. L4 axons rarely leave the local area.
Role: a feedforward entry stage. In the Thousand Brains framework L4 is where sensory features are associated with locations (see "Sensorimotor Object Recognition" in section 5).

Contents: the largest pyramidal cells of the cortex. Two broad classes matter for modelling: thick-tufted, intrinsically bursting cells (often in L5b), whose apical tuft spans L1, and slender-tufted, regular-spiking intratelencephalic (IT) cells (often in L5a).

Outputs of thick-tufted cells (extratelencephalic or pyramidal-tract type): brainstem, spinal cord, superior colliculus, striatum and higher-order thalamus (e.g. POm, pulvinar). In motor cortex these include the corticospinal neurons; Betz cells are an extreme example.
Outputs of IT cells: other cortical areas (including the opposite hemisphere) and the striatum.
Inputs: L2/3 (strong), L4, L5 itself, L6, thalamus, and apical-tuft input in L1.

Role: the column's 'action' output. Hawkins and colleagues note that every cortical region, including primary sensory areas, has L5 cells projecting to motor-related structures — part of their argument that every column is a sensorimotor model.
Contents: corticothalamic (CT) pyramidal cells, IT cells and a heterogeneous population of other shapes; L6b (subplate remnant) at the bottom.

Outputs: CT cells project back to the thalamic nucleus that feeds the column and to the thalamic reticular nucleus. In the LGN, synapses from L6 outnumber retinal synapses on relay cells — a strong hint that this pathway modulates rather than drives (see "Thalamocortical Loops").
Inputs: thalamus (directly), L4, L5, L6, and other cortical areas.

Role: gain control and gating of thalamic transmission; in the Thousand Brains theory L6 is proposed to carry a location signal analogous to grid cells (see "Grid and Displacement Cells" in section 5). That proposal is a hypothesis, not established physiology.

blocks.text: The canonical flow and its shortcuts

The textbook pathway in primary sensory cortex is thalamus → L4 → L2/3 → L5 → L6 → thalamus, with L2/3 also sending output to other areas and L5 to subcortical targets. Douglas & Martin (2004) and Thomson & Lamy (2007) review this flow; Binzegger, Douglas & Martin (2004) quantified it in cat V1 by counting synapses. Two refinements matter in practice. First, the thalamus also directly contacts L5 and L6 neurons: Constantinople & Bruno (2013) showed that deep layers respond to whisker input even when upper layers are silenced, so the cortex is better seen as two partly parallel strata (upper and deep) than as a strict serial chain. Second, a large fraction of each layer's excitatory input is recurrent within the layer, so a model where each layer is just a feedforward stage misses most of the synapses.

blocks.source:
Simplified excitatory pathways in a primary sensory column

  higher areas ──feedback──► L1 (apical tufts)          matrix thalamus ─► L1
  core thalamus ──driver──► L4 ──► L2/3 ──► other cortical areas (feedforward)
        │                           │
        └──────────► L5/L6          ▼
                                   L5 ──► brainstem, spinal cord, striatum,
                                    │     higher-order thalamus
                                    ▼
                                   L6 ──► same thalamic nucleus + TRN (feedback)

Approximate share of neurons per layer under 1 mm² (Potjans & Diesmann 2014,
based on cat/rat data): L2/3 ≈ 34%, L4 ≈ 36%, L5 ≈ 8%, L6 ≈ 22%
(excitatory and inhibitory combined; L1 omitted; ≈ 77,000 neurons in total).

blocks.text: The percentages above come from one specific data-driven model; they vary by species and area and you should treat them as a starting point, not a law. In primate V1, L4 is subdivided (4A, 4B, 4Cα, 4Cβ) and much thicker; in motor cortex L5 is especially large.
Regional variation: not all cortex has six obvious layers

The six-layer scheme is a template, and areas modify it. Primary motor cortex (and much of frontal cortex) is traditionally called agranular because it lacks a clearly visible L4 under the microscope. Yamawaki et al. (2014) showed that mouse motor cortex nonetheless contains a thin layer of L4-like neurons that receive thalamic input and project to L2/3, so 'agranular' means 'L4 reduced', not necessarily 'L4 absent'. Conversely, primary visual cortex in primates is hypergranular, with an elaborate L4. Layer thicknesses, cell densities and the balance of feedforward versus feedback connections differ systematically across the cortical hierarchy; Harris & Shepherd (2015) review these 'themes and variations'.

Feedforward versus feedback by layer: projections going up the hierarchy tend to originate in supragranular layers and terminate in L4, while projections going down tend to originate in infragranular layers and avoid L4, terminating in L1 and L6. This rule, derived from primate visual cortex, is how anatomists assign areas to hierarchical levels. It is a strong statistical tendency rather than an absolute rule.
What this means for your model

items: Keep at least four excitatory populations if you want laminar structure to mean anything: L4 (input), L2/3 (cortico-cortical, sparse), L5 (output, ideally with a two-compartment or apical-input mechanism) and L6 (feedback to your thalamus or input stage). Each with its own inhibitory population — the Potjans–Diesmann 8-population layout is a well-tested template (see "Potjans–Diesmann Microcircuit" in section 6).
Merging L2 and L3 is standard and safe. Merging L5 and L6 loses the distinction between action output and thalamic feedback, which matters for any sensorimotor or Thousand Brains-style model.

L1 does not need neurons in most models; model it as a distinct input channel onto apical dendrites (a separate compartment, dendritic segment or multiplicative gain) rather than as extra somatic current.
Route thalamic input to L4 and, more weakly, to L5/L6 directly. A pure serial chain makes deep layers wait for upper layers and distorts timing.

Make most excitatory input recurrent within and between layers, with thalamic input a minority of synapses but strong and synchronous. If your L4 only responds when you give it huge feedforward weights, compare against this biology.
Target low firing rates: L2/3 pyramidal cells around 0.1–2 Hz spontaneously; deep-layer cells a few Hz. Rates far above that usually signal missing inhibition (see "Cell Types").
Decide whether you are modelling a granular sensory area or an agranular motor area; the input layer you emphasise depends on it.
